questions.q: In « Je m'en vais », what does en replace?
choices: the place you are going to
questions.why: This is the difference from Chapter 10. In j'en ai besoin the en is recoverable; in s'en aller it replaces nothing and the verb is learned whole, pronoun included.
Ça y est is fixed: that's it, done. The y points at nothing in particular, which is what makes it an idiom rather than a replacement.

questions.q: Complete with the right pronoun: « Ne t'___ fais pas, ça ira. »
questions.why: S'en faire means to worry, and the en is part of the verb. Ne te fais pas is not French.

questions.q: How do you say « He holds it against me » ?
questions.why: En vouloir à quelqu'un takes an indirect object, so the person becomes me / te / lui / leur, never à + stressed pronoun. The person pronoun comes first, en last.

questions.q: Complete: « Tu t'___ prends mal. » (You're going about it the wrong way.)
questions.why: S'y prendre is a y expression. Compare s'en prendre à quelqu'un, which is a different verb entirely: to take it out on someone.

choices: Dans ce livre, il s'agit de la guerre.
Ce livre s'agit de la guerre.
Il s'agit ce livre de la guerre.
questions.why: S'agir is impersonal: its subject can only be il. A book cannot s'agir of anything. The alternative is ce livre parle de la guerre.

questions.q: Put s'en aller in the tu imperative: « ___ ! » (Go away!)
questions.why: Positive command: pronouns go behind, joined by hyphens, and te becomes t' before en. The -s of vas drops in the imperative of aller.

questions.q: « Elle ___ sans rien dire. » (She left without saying a thing.)
questions.why: S'en aller takes être, the participle agrees with the subject, and both pronouns stay in front of the auxiliary — never wrapped around the participle.

questions.q: Complete: « Je n'___ suis pour rien. » (It's nothing to do with me.)
questions.why: N'y être pour rien is the standard way to deny responsibility. Je n'en suis pour rien does not exist.

questions.q: « J'en ai pour dix minutes » means:
choices: I've had it for ten minutes.
I want ten minutes of it.
questions.why: En avoir pour + a length of time is how French says how long something will take you. Nothing in it is deducible from the parts.

questions.q: Someone thanks you. Which reply is wrong?
choices: Il n'y a pas de quoi.
questions.why: Prier quelqu'un de quelque chose gives en, not y. Je t'en prie is the tu version, and de rien is the everyday spoken one.
A negative command drops the hyphens and puts the pronouns back in front of the verb, in the normal order.
The pronouns belong to the infinitive and travel with it, so they sit between the conjugated aller and m'en aller — not before vais.

questions.q: Complete: « J'___ ai marre de ce bruit. »
questions.why: En avoir marre de is fixed. Same shape as en avoir assez de and ne plus en pouvoir, all of which keep en whatever follows.
En valoir la peine — to be worth it. The en carries no meaning of its own, which is why it is easy to drop when writing it down.

questions.q: Say it out loud: you'll get used to it.
questions.why: S'y faire, in the futur simple of faire. The t' and y run together as one sound, which is what makes these idioms hard to catch in speech.

questions.q: Give three fixed expressions built on en and three built on y, with a translation each.
a: en: s'en aller (to leave), en vouloir à qqn (to hold a grudge), s'en sortir (to manage) — also s'en faire, en avoir marre, en valoir la peine. y: ça y est (that's it), s'y prendre (to go about it), s'y connaître (to know one's way around) — also y tenir, s'y faire, n'y être pour rien.
questions.why: The point of the chapter is that these are vocabulary, not grammar. If you can list them cold, you have done the work.
